drug_class: MAO-B inhibitor (monoamine oxidase type B inhibitor)
purpose: Rasagiline is used to treat Parkinson's disease. It can be used on its own in early Parkinson's or added to other Parkinson's medications like levodopa when symptoms are harder to control. It helps reduce symptoms like tremors, stiffness, and slowness of movement.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical called dopamine to help control smooth movement. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine levels are too low. Rasagiline works by blocking an enzyme called MAO-B that normally breaks down dopamine, so more dopamine stays available in your brain. This helps your body move more smoothly and comfortably.
common_side_effects: Headache, joint pain, upset stomach or nausea, dizziness, feeling tired, flu-like symptoms, and in some people a runny nose or skin rash. If you are also taking levodopa, you may notice more involuntary movements or feel lightheaded when standing up.
warnings: This medication has serious interactions with many other drugs — especially antidepressants (like SSRIs, SNRIs, or tricyclics), certain pain medicines like tramadol or meperidine, and other MAO inhibitors. Combining these can cause a dangerous reaction called serotonin syndrome. You must avoid foods very high in tyramine (like aged cheeses, cured meats, or tap beer) in large amounts. Tell ALL your doctors and pharmacists you take this medication. Do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 0.5 mg or 1 mg taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on whether you are taking other Parkinson's medications. It can be taken with or without food, and it is easiest to remember if you take it at the same time each day.
